Data commands are local-first (`--backend local`, default) or remote (`--backend mcp`), with readable tables, `--json`, and a top-level `score`. | | **`connectors/`** (`agentic-odi-connectors`) | Pluggable external integrations. The first kind is an **MCP client connector** that connects to a remote MCP server over HTTP, checks health, and ingests tools/resources into a local ingest sink. Additional kinds (REST, webhooks, and so on) can register against the same protocol later. | --- ## 🚀 Getting Started ### Prerequisites - **Python** 3.10+ - [**uv**](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) package manager Install the entire workspace (all six projects plus dev tooling): ```bash uv sync --all-packages ``` This creates a `.venv` and installs `agentic-odi-core`, `agentic-odi-mcp-server`, `agentic-odi-local-server`, `agentic-odi-client`, `agentic-odi-cli`, and `agentic-odi-connectors` in editable mode. ### 💻 Command-Line Interface (CLI) The [`Typer`](https://github.com/fastapi/typer)-based CLI lets you interact with Agentic ODI directly from your terminal. It provides an interactive chat mode plus version, update, and data commands. Data commands are **local-first**: they read and write a SQLite store with no server required, and switch to a remote MCP server with `--backend mcp`. Launch it with: ```bash python -m cli --version # print the Agentic ODI version python -m cli --help # show available options and commands python -m cli # start interactive chat in a terminal (help when piped) ``` A console script is also installed, so `agentic-odi --version` works the same way. **Global options:** | Option | Environment variable | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---|---| | `--backend local\|mcp` | `AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND` | `local` | Run in-process against SQLite, or call a remote MCP server. | | `--db PATH` | `AGENTIC_ODI_DB` | `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db` | Store path for the `local` backend. | | `--mcp-url URL` | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` | Server URL for the `mcp` backend. | Data commands print readable tables and blocks by default; add `--json` for machine-readable output. Diagnostics go to stderr and failures exit non-zero (`0` success, `1` error, `2` usage error). ### 💬 Interactive Chat `agentic-odi chat` (or simply `agentic-odi` in a terminal) starts a conversational session against the MCP server and an OpenAI-compatible LLM. Responses stream to the terminal, and the assistant can call the ODI MCP tools as it talks. ```bash agentic-odi chat agentic-odi chat --model local-tools-model --mcp-url http://localhost:8000/mcp ``` Before starting, run the MCP server (`python -m mcp_server`) and point the chat at an OpenAI-compatible model endpoint. The chat reads the same environment variables as the Living Studio: | Variable | Default | CLI flag | |---|---|---| | `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:8001/v1` | `--base-url` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL` | `local-tools-model` | `--model` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY` | `local` | `--api-key` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` | `--mcp-url` | Inside the session, `/help` lists the commands, `/tools` lists the MCP tools the assistant can call, `/clear` resets the conversation, and `/exit` (or `/quit`) ends the session. > [!NOTE] > Chat is the only CLI mode that needs an LLM endpoint. The `customer-outcomes` and `connectors` commands keep working without one. ### 🎯 Manage Customer Outcomes Customer Outcomes link customer value to business value. The `local` backend writes to the shared SQLite store with no server required; add `--backend mcp` to route through a running MCP server (`python -m mcp_server`). The group is also available under its historical name `outcomes`. ```bash # Add a Customer Outcome agentic-odi customer-outcomes add --job-id --direction minimize --unit "time" --object "to resolve setup errors" --statement "Minimize the time to resolve environment setup errors when onboarding" --importance 8.8 --satisfaction 3.2 --category cost_reduction --business-statement "Saves engineering hours and reduces early churn" # List outcomes (optionally filtered, or as JSON) agentic-odi customer-outcomes list agentic-odi customer-outcomes list --job-id agentic-odi customer-outcomes list --json # Get, update, delete agentic-odi customer-outcomes get agentic-odi customer-outcomes update --importance 9.0 agentic-odi customer-outcomes delete --yes # Compute ODI Opportunity Score (top-level, also under the group) agentic-odi score 8 2 agentic-odi outcomes score 8 2 ``` Set `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` (or `--mcp-url`) to point to a non-default server when using `--backend mcp`. ### 🔌 External Connectors (MCP Ingest) Connectors are named integrations stored in `.agentic-odi/connectors.json` (or a path you pass with `--config` / `AGENTIC_ODI_CONNECTORS_FILE`). The first kind is `mcp`: Agentic ODI acts as an MCP **client** and pulls catalog, resources, and optional tool results from an external MCP **server**. The fastest way to connect is a preset. `connectors catalog` lists every built-in preset, grouped by the capability area it serves: ```bash python -m cli connectors catalog # all presets python -m cli connectors catalog --area strategy-alignment python -m cli connectors catalog --json ``` | Capability area (`--area`) | Presets | |---|---| | Voice of customer & qualitative research (`voice-of-customer`) | `notion`, `gong`, `fireflies`, `intercom`, `confluence` | | Quantitative data & opportunity scoring (`quantitative-data`) | `posthog`, `amplitude`, `mixpanel` | | Market & competitive intelligence (`market-intelligence`) | `exa`, `tavily` | | Product strategy & backlog alignment (`strategy-alignment`) | `linear`, `github`, `jira`, `miro`, `figma` | | Strategy & knowledge management output (`knowledge-output`) | `slack` | Register one with `--preset`; `--name` defaults to the preset id: ```bash # Token-based preset: export the variable it needs first export GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN=ghp_... python -m cli connectors add mcp --preset github python -m cli connectors health --name github python -m cli connectors ingest --name github # OAuth-based preset: the browser consent flow starts on first use python -m cli connectors add mcp --preset notion ``` Credentials never enter the registry. Presets that use API keys store `${VAR}` placeholders that are resolved from the environment when a connection is opened, and `connectors health` names any variable that is missing. `--url` overrides the endpoint (self-hosted or proxied deployments) and `--tool` still selects which tools to call during ingest. Custom servers keep working the same way: ```bash python -m cli connectors add mcp --name internal --url https://mcp.internal.example/mcp --tool latest_quote python -m cli connectors list ``` Ingested records are normalized (`catalog`, `resource`, `tool_result`) and appended to the in-process ingest sink. They are not written into the ODI jobs/outcomes store. > [!NOTE] > Presets cover MCP servers with a hosted endpoint. Servers you run yourself (Snowflake, BigQuery, Google Drive, Brave Search, and similar) are added with an explicit `--url`. The catalog lives in `connectors/src/connectors/catalog.py`. > [!NOTE] > OAuth tokens are cached in memory for the life of one CLI process, so an OAuth preset may ask for consent again on the next `connectors health` or `connectors ingest`. Prefer a token-based preset where the server offers one. ### ⚡ Living Studio Run Modes The Living Studio runs three ways. All of them serve the same SPA, which talks only to the sidecar on `http://127.0.0.1:8100` — the SPA never contacts MCP or the LLM directly. **Architecture** ```text ┌────────────────────────────┐ /api (JSON) ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ Living Studio SPA │ ────────────▶ │ local_server (sidecar) │ │ React + TS + Vite │ /api/chat │ FastAPI on 127.0.0.1:8100 │ │ (browser or Tauri webview)│ ◀──────────── │ - config / health / canvas │ └────────────────────────────┘ SSE stream │ - steps / outcomes (via MCP) │ │ - /api/chat (LLM tool-loop) │ └───────────────┬───────────────┘ │ MCP (HTTP) ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ mcp_server :8000/mcp │ └───────────────────────────────┘ ▲ │ OpenAI-compatible ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐ │ Your local LLM backend │ └───────────────────────────────┘ ``` **1. Web — production build (recommended for a quick look)** ```bash npm --prefix studio run build # build the SPA into studio/dist python -m client.run # starts MCP :8000 + sidecar :8100 ``` | Service | URL | |---|---| | MCP Server | http://localhost:8000/mcp | | Living Studio | http://127.0.0.1:8100 | **2. Web — dev with hot reload** (Vite proxies `/api` to the sidecar): ```bash npm --prefix studio run dev:full # MCP + sidecar + Vite together # open http://localhost:5173 ``` **3. Desktop — Tauri 2** (the app spawns the MCP server and sidecar itself): ```bash npm --prefix studio run tauri dev # dev window npm --prefix studio run tauri build # bundles: .deb / .AppImage (Linux), .app / .dmg (macOS), .msi / .exe (Windows) ``` > [!NOTE] > **Tauri prerequisites.** The desktop build needs the WebKitGTK toolchain and Rust 1.90+. On Debian/Ubuntu: > > ```bash > sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev build-essential pkg-config curl wget file \ > libxdo-dev libssl-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf xdg-utils libfuse2t64 > ``` > > The Tauri CLI ships as the `@tauri-apps/cli` npm dev dependency (`npm --prefix studio run tauri`). The sidecar is launched with `uv run python -m …` from the repository root; if the app cannot locate the repo root, set `AGENTIC_ODI_REPO_ROOT`. #### 🔐 Desktop signing & updater secrets Self-updating and code signing are **env-driven**: if a secret is absent, an unsigned artifact is produced instead of failing. CI reads these from GitHub Actions secrets. | Secret | Purpose | |---|---| | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` | Signs updater artifacts (`.sig`) and the `latest.json` manifest. A tagged release fails loudly without it. Generate with `npm --prefix studio run tauri signer generate`. | | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD` | Password for the private key (optional when the key has none). | | `APPLE_CERTIFICATE` / `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | macOS Developer ID certificate (base64 `.p12`) and its password. | | `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` | macOS signing identity. | | `APPLE_ID` / `APPLE_PASSWORD` / `APPLE_TEAM_ID` | macOS notarization credentials. | | `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE` / `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | Windows Authenticode PFX (base64) and its password; imported by CI and injected into the bundle config. | Releases are published by `.github/workflows/tauri-release.yml` when a `v*` tag is pushed. The desktop app checks for updates on startup and via **Settings → Check for updates**. #### 🔑 Managing the updater signing key The updater key pair authenticates release artifacts so an installed app can verify that an auto-update genuinely came from you. The **public** key is embedded in `studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` (`plugins.updater.pubkey`) and is safe to commit. The **private** key must never be committed, logged, printed in CI, or attached to a build artifact. 1. **Generate a key pair** (only if you need a new one). Leave `-p ""` for a passwordless key, or pass a password and remember it: ```bash npm --prefix studio run tauri signer generate -- -w ./living-studio.key -p "" -f ``` This writes `living-studio.key` (private, `0600`) and `living-studio.key.pub` (public). 2. **Paste the public key** into `studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`: ```jsonc { "plugins": { "updater": { "endpoints": ["https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/latest.json"], "pubkey": "" } } } ``` 3. **Store the private key outside the repository** (the repo root is git-tracked; a sibling directory is not), with restricted permissions: ```bash mkdir -p ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys && chmod 700 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys mv living-studio.key ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/ chmod 600 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key ``` Move it to a long-term secret store (password manager, 1Password/Bitwarden/Vault, or a private encrypted backup) when you decide where that lives. Losing it means future releases can no longer be signed for existing installs. 4. **Add the private key as a GitHub Actions secret** (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret), or via the CLI: ```bash gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY < ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD --body "" # only if you set a password ``` 5. **Verify** the secrets exist (values are never displayed): ```bash gh secret list ``` 6. **Rotate** by repeating steps 1–4, then publishing a release signed with the new key. Existing installs still verify against the public key compiled into their binary, so keep the old private key usable and publish the new public key ahead of the cut-over. > [!CAUTION] > If the private key leaks, treat auto-updates as compromised: generate a new pair, rotate the Actions secret, and publish a freshly signed release. > [!IMPORTANT] > **Migration note.** The Streamlit UI (`client/src/client/app.py`) has been removed. The Living Studio now lives in `studio/` (browser SPA + Tauri desktop app) and is served by the `local_server` sidecar on port **8100** (previously Streamlit's `8501`). Start everything with `python -m client.run`. All `AGENTIC_ODI_*` environment variable names, the demo dataset, and the ODI formulas are unchanged. ### 🧠 Local Tools-Capable LLM Backend (for MCP testing) To exercise real tool-calling end-to-end against the MCP server, you need a local LLM backend that: - Exposes an **OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API** (for example, `/v1/chat/completions`), and - Supports OpenAI-style **`tools` / `tool_calls`**. A simple fully local option is [`llama-cpp-python`](https://github.com/abetlen/llama-cpp-python), which can run a quantized model on your machine and expose an OpenAI-compatible server. 1. **Install a local LLM server** Install `llama-cpp-python` in your environment (see its README for platform-specific build notes): ```bash pip install llama-cpp-python ``` 2. **Download a small tools-capable model** Download a small GGUF model that supports function/tool calling (for example, a 7B function-calling variant from Hugging Face) and note its path, e.g. `C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf`. 3. **Start the OpenAI-compatible server** Start the server and give the model a friendly alias that matches the default used by the Living Studio sidecar: ```bash python -m llama_cpp.server \ --model "C:\models\local-tools-model.gguf" \ --model_alias local-tools-model \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001 \ --chat_format openai ``` This exposes an OpenAI-style API at `http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1`. 4. **Point the Living Studio at the local server** The sidecar reads defaults from environment variables (with sensible fallbacks): | Variable | Default | |---|---| | `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:8001/v1` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL` | `local-tools-model` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` | | `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY` | `local` | You can either set these in your shell or adjust them in the Living Studio's **Settings** panel. 5. **Verify tool-calling against the MCP server** - (Optional) Before starting the UI, confirm the LLM backend is reachable: ```bash curl http://127.0.0.1:8001/v1/models ``` If this request fails, fix your local LLM server configuration before debugging the MCP client/server. - Start the MCP server and the Living Studio (via `python -m client.run` or `npm --prefix studio run dev:full`). - In the browser UI, ask the assistant something that should use ODI tools, for example: “Help me define a new Job-to-be-Done and add it to your ODI repository.” - You should see the assistant briefly display that it is calling tools (for example, `add_job`, `get_jobs`, etc.) and then respond with grounded ODI guidance, confirming that the local LLM, MCP server, and client wiring all work together. - If the LLM backend is unreachable or misconfigured, the UI will show a clear error banner indicating that the backend at your configured **Base URL** could not be reached, along with details from the underlying error. Use that message together with the steps above to fix your local LLM setup. ### 🤖 Agent-Driven Testing Type `/dev` in the AI assistant to trigger the full automated workflow: it will start both processes, open the browser, send a test message, and report the results. --- ## 🧹 Linting, Formatting & Type Checks (CI parity) The CI pipeline runs several quality checks. You can mirror them locally with: ```bash # Ruff lint and formatting checks (per-file config comes from each project's pyproject.toml) uv run ruff check . uv run ruff format --check . # Type checking (run per project so each project's config applies) uv run --directory core mypy . uv run --directory mcp_server mypy . uv run --directory local_server mypy . uv run --directory client mypy . uv run --directory cli mypy . uv run --directory connectors mypy . # Security scanning uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r core/src mcp_server/src local_server/src cli/src client/src connectors/src # Tests (same as CI) uv run --directory core pytest uv run --directory mcp_server pytest uv run --directory local_server pytest uv run --directory client pytest uv run --directory cli pytest uv run --directory connectors pytest ``` ### 🖥️ Frontend & Desktop Checks (studio) The SPA and Tauri shell mirror their CI jobs locally: ```bash npm --prefix studio run lint # ESLint npm --prefix studio run typecheck # tsc --noEmit npm --prefix studio test -- --run # Vitest (run once) npm --prefix studio run build # production build → studio/dist cd studio/src-tauri && cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy -- -D warnings && cargo check ``` To run these automatically before each commit, enable the bundled pre-commit hooks: ```bash uv tool install pre-commit pre-commit install ``` After this, `ruff` and `ruff-format` will run on staged files whenever you commit. COVERAGE_FILE="$PWD/.coverage.$pkg" uv run --directory "$pkg" pytest --cov="$pkg" -q done uv run coverage combine .coverage.* uv run coverage xml -o coverage.xml && uv run coverage report ``` > Install the latest release with one command: ```bash curl -fsSL https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh ``` The installer places the binary under `~/.local/share/agentic-odi/versions//`, creates a `current` symlink, and symlinks `odi`, `odipm`, `odi-cli`, and `agentic-odi` into `~/.local/bin/`. If `~/.local/bin` is not on your PATH, add it (e.g., `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"`). On Windows, the PowerShell installer uses `~\AppData\Local\agentic-odi\` and copies `.exe` files to `~\AppData\Local\agentic-odi\bin\`. ### Update By default, `odi` auto-checks for updates once every 24 hours and applies the update on the next run (auto-update is enabled by default). Control behavior with: - `odi update` — explicit check and update - `--no-update` flag — skip auto-update for this run - `AGENTIC_ODI_NO_UPDATE=1` — disable auto-update globally When running from a non-frozen source install, auto-update is suppressed automatically. ### Install layout ``` ~/.local/share/agentic-odi/ ├── versions// │ └── odi (and bundled files) └── current -> versions/ ~/.local/bin/ ├── odi -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi ├── odipm ├── odi-cli └── agentic-odi ~/.config/agentic-odi/ # state/preferences ``` Environment variables: `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR` (override install root), `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_BIN_HOME`. The default backend is `local` (`--backend local`); no MCP server is required. ### Unsigned binaries macOS may quarantine downloaded binaries: `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ~/.local/bin/odi` (if needed). Windows SmartScreen may show a warning for unsigned binaries; choose "More info → Run anyway" if you trust the release. ### Release automation Releases are cut and published by CI with no approval step: 1. Conventional commits land on `main`; `release-please` opens or updates the release PR. 2. The `release-please` workflow arms auto-merge on that PR. `main` requires the `CI green` check (ruleset `main-requires-ci-green`), so the PR merges itself as soon as CI passes — nobody clicks merge. 3. The merge cuts tag `vX.Y.Z` and the GitHub Release; the tag starts the `release` and `Tauri Release` workflows, which attach the CLI archives, `checksums.txt`, the install scripts, and the desktop bundles to it. 4. `e2e-install` runs after `release` succeeds and installs the published binary on Linux, macOS, and Windows. **One-time setup (GitHub App).** GitHub holds workflow runs that start from `GITHUB_TOKEN`-authored pushes ("This workflow requires approval from a maintainer") and ignores the tag such a push creates, which is why releases used to need a maintainer. A release-only GitHub App avoids both: 1. Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App, with permissions: Contents `Read and write`, Issues `Read and write`, Pull requests `Read and write` (no webhook). 2. Install the App on this repository. 3. Add repository secrets `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID` (the App's client ID) and `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` (a generated private key). Until those secrets exist, the `release-please` workflow logs a warning and falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN`: releases still happen, but the release PR needs a maintainer approval and merge, and the tag will not start the asset builds. After adding the secrets, re-run the workflow (`gh workflow run release-please.yml`) or push to `main` so the open release PR is re-driven by the App. To check the installer without cutting a release, run `bash scripts/tests/install_e2e.sh` — it serves a simulated release over HTTP and exercises `scripts/install.sh` end to end (CI runs it too). ## ☁️ Deployment The server is deployed via **[Horizon Prefect](https://www.prefect.io/horizon)**, Prefect's managed infrastructure for hosting MCP-compatible agents. ### 🧪 Test Chat (UI) Interact with the deployed agent directly in your browser: > **[https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat](https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat)** ### 🔌 MCP Server Endpoint Integrate via the MCP protocol at: > **[https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp](https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp)** > [!IMPORTANT] > **Authentication is required** to access the MCP server endpoint. Please reach out to the maintainers to obtain the necessary credentials before connecting a client. --- ## 🗺️ Roadmap & Next Steps As we validate the feasibility of this architecture, our next milestones include: - [x] **External MCP client connector**: Pluggable connectors package with an HTTP MCP ingest client, CLI adapter, and in-memory tests. - [ ] **Map ingested evidence onto ODI artifacts**: Turn connector records into jobs, outcomes, or evidence without mixing connector plumbing into the ODI store. - [ ] **Additional connector kinds**: REST/webhooks and similar integrations implementing the same `Connector` protocol. - [ ] **ODI Schema Definition**: Define standardized Pydantic models for *Jobs*, *Steps*, and *Outcomes*. - [x] **CLI Dataset Commands**: Extend `cli/` so the ODI dataset can be created, queried, and scored from the terminal, in addition to the current MCP path. - [ ] **Context Tooling**: Replace the dummy `greet` tool with capabilities like `get_job_map(job_id)` or `evaluate_outcome(statement)`. - [ ] **Data Persistence Layer**: Connect the fastmcp server to a lightweight vector or relational database containing actual user research data. - [ ] **Agentic Integration**: Hook the client up to an LLM (e.g., via LangChain or standard OpenAI clients) so the LLM can *discover* the ODI tools and intelligently request customer insights when ideating features. --- ## 🤝 Contributing Contributions are welcome! This project uses [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) for linting and formatting and [pytest](https://pytest.org/) for tests. Please ensure any change passes the [lint, format, and test checks](#-linting-formatting--type-checks-ci-parity) before opening a pull request. --- ## 📄 License No license has been specified for this repository yet. --- apps/studio-api/src/agentic_odi_studio_api/studio/transcribe.py	
+++ apps/studio-api/src/agentic_odi_studio_api/studio/transcribe.py	
@@ -1,130 +0,0 @@
-"""Speech-to-text for the Living Studio's voice input.
-
-The sidecar owns this path so the SPA never holds a route to the model
-backend. Audio arrives as a multipart upload, is forwarded to the
-OpenAI-compatible ``/audio/transcriptions`` endpoint, and comes back as text.
-
-The credentials are the sidecar's own (see :func:`defaults`), never the
-client's. The sidecar is an unauthenticated local service, so a client-supplied
-``base_url`` would turn this endpoint into a request relay pointed wherever the
-caller named.
-"""
-
-from __future__ import annotations
-
-from openai import AsyncOpenAI
-
-# 20 MB is roughly half an hour of opus audio. A spoken product intent is
-# seconds. The cap exists to stop a runaway recording from becoming an
-# unbounded upload, not to ration speech.
-MAX_AUDIO_BYTES = 20 * 1024 * 1024
-
-TRANSCRIPTION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 30.0
-
-# The OpenAI-compatible transcription API identifies the audio format from the
-# filename extension and the content type, so both must be one it knows.
-SUPPORTED_MIME_TYPES: dict[str, str] = {
-    "audio/webm": ".webm",
-    "audio/webm;codecs=opus": ".webm",
-    "audio/ogg": ".ogg",
-    "audio/ogg;codecs=opus": ".ogg",
-    "audio/mp4": ".mp4",
-    "audio/mpeg": ".mp3",
-    "audio/mpga": ".mpga",
-    "audio/wav": ".wav",
-    "audio/x-wav": ".wav",
-    "audio/flac": ".flac",
-    "audio/m4a": ".m4a",
-}
-
-
-class TranscriptionError(Exception):
-    """A transcription that could not be completed, with the status to report."""
-
-    def __init__(self, status_code: int, detail: str) -> None:
-        super().__init__(detail)
-        self.status_code = status_code
-        self.detail = detail
-
-
-def audio_filename(mime_type: str) -> str:
-    """Name the upload so the backend can identify the audio format.
-
-    The extension matters as much as the content type: the OpenAI-compatible
-    API infers the codec from the filename.
-    """
-    normalized = mime_type.split(";")[0].strip().lower()
-    extension = SUPPORTED_MIME_TYPES.get(normalized) or SUPPORTED_MIME_TYPES.get(
-        mime_type.strip().lower(), ""
-    )
-    return f"recording{extension}"
-
-
-def _validate(audio: bytes, mime_type: str) -> None:
-    if not audio:
-        raise TranscriptionError(400, "The recording was empty.")
-    if len(audio) > MAX_AUDIO_BYTES:
-        raise TranscriptionError(
-            413,
-            f"The recording is larger than the {MAX_AUDIO_BYTES // (1024 * 1024)} MB limit.",
-        )
-    normalized = mime_type.split(";")[0].strip().lower()
-    if normalized not in SUPPORTED_MIME_TYPES:
-        raise TranscriptionError(
-            415,
-            f"Unsupported audio type '{mime_type}'. "
-            f"Supported: {', '.join(sorted(SUPPORTED_MIME_TYPES))}.",
-        )
-
-
-async def transcribe_audio(
-    audio: bytes,
-    mime_type: str,
-    model: str,
-    base_url: str,
-    api_key: str,
-) -> str:
-    """Transcribe recorded audio and return the spoken text.
-
-    Args:
-        audio: The raw recorded bytes.
-        mime_type: The content type the browser recorded, e.g. ``audio/webm``.
-        model: The transcription model to use, e.g. ``whisper-1``.
-        base_url: The OpenAI-compatible base URL of the model backend.
-        api_key: The API key for that backend.
-
-    Raises:
-        TranscriptionError: The recording was unusable (400, 413, 415) or the
-            backend refused the request (502). The backend's own message is
-            preserved, because a misconfigured ``base_url`` is the most likely
-            failure and the user needs the backend's words to fix it.
-    """
-    _validate(audio, mime_type)
-
-    client = AsyncOpenAI(
-        base_url=base_url,
-        api_key=api_key,
-        timeout=TRANSCRIPTION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
-    )
-    try:
-        result = await client.audio.transcriptions.create(
-            file=(audio_filename(mime_type), audio, mime_type),
-            model=model,
-            response_format="text",
-        )
-    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
-        raise TranscriptionError(
-            502, f"The transcription backend rejected the recording: {exc}"
-        ) from exc
-
-    text = result if isinstance(result, str) else getattr(result, "text", "")
-    return text.strip()
-
-
-__all__ = [
-    "MAX_AUDIO_BYTES",
-    "SUPPORTED_MIME_TYPES",
-    "TranscriptionError",
-    "audio_filename",
-    "transcribe_audio",
-]

-# Living Studio: Intent-First Product Management
-
-The Living Studio is an interactive, conversational environment for product managers to focus on their career-defining opportunities. It leverages Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect the product manager's intent with outcome-driven innovation.
-
-## The Vision
-
-The Living Studio has been redesigned to focus on **product managers' ambition** rather than ODI methodology. The agent now interprets PMs' career-defining opportunities and helps them win them, rather than explaining frameworks.
-
-**North Star:** Help me choose and win the next opportunity that matters — to customers, the business, and my career.
-
-## Key Features
-
-1. **Intent-First Agent**: The system prompt has been rewritten to prioritize PM ambition and silent translation of ODI concepts into actionable outcomes. The agent now proposes observations and asks for confirmation, creating a "living memory" of the conversation.
-
-2. **Local Studio Memory**: A SQLite-backed store persists conversations and observations (`career`, `opportunity`, `business`, etc.) across sessions. The "What I've learned" panel shows these observations and allows the PM to confirm, edit, or dismiss them.
-
-3. **Opportunity Thesis**: The default canvas focus is the **Opportunity Thesis** card, which presents one opportunity with its importance, current state, and the gap to be closed. This replaces the traditional Opportunity Landscape.
-
-4. **Ambition-Driven Onboarding**: The first-run wizard now presents four doors based on the PM's intent:
-   - "I have an opportunity in mind"
-   - "My boss handed me a priority"
-   - "I need to find one"
-   - "Pressure-test an idea"
-
-5. **Session Persistence**: Conversations are persisted via the `conversationId` and `memory` SSE events, allowing the PM to resume from where they left off.
-
-6. **Explainability**: The agent uses a `remember` tool to propose observations, which are stored in the local memory store and displayed in the MemoryPanel.
-
-## How to Use
-
-1. **Start the Living Studio**:
-   ```bash
-   python -m client.run
-   ```
-   This launches the MCP server and the Studio sidecar.
-
-2. **Access the Studio**:
-   Open your browser at `http://127.0.0.1:8100`.
-
-3. **Interact**:
-   - The agent will greet you and ask about your intent.
-   - Use the chat interface to discuss your opportunity.
-   - The agent will propose observations and ask for confirmation.
-   - Review the "What I've learned" panel to see your conversation history.
-
-4. **Persist Your Work**:
-   The Studio automatically saves your conversation and observations. They will be available the next time you start the application.
-
-## Technical Details
-
-- **Backend**: FastAPI with FastMCP integration.
-- **Database**: SQLite (local storage at `~/.agentic-odi/studio.db`).
-- **Frontend**: React with TypeScript and Vite.
-- **Agent**: Local tools-capable LLM backend (e.g., llama-cpp-python) with OpenAI-compatible API.
-
-## Contributing
-
-If you'd like to contribute to the Living Studio, please refer to the main repository's contributing guidelines.

<skill_content name="brainstorming">
# Skill: brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

131:             "function": {

146:             "Register an external MCP or REST connector into the shared connector "
147:             "registry so the Living Studio and CLI can use it. Provide a 'preset' "
148:             "id (from connectors catalog) and optionally a 'name' and 'url' "
149:             "override, or a custom 'name' + 'url'. Does not require an MCP server."
150:         ),
151:         "parameters": {
152:             "type": "object",
153:             "properties": {
154:                 "name": {
155:                     "type": "string",
156:                     "description": "Unique connector name (defaults to the preset id).",
157:                 },
158:                 "preset": {
159:                     "type": "string",
160:                     "description": "Preset id, e.g. notion, posthog, exa, linear, github.",
161:                 },
162:                 "url": {
163:                     "type": "string",
164:                     "description": "Custom endpoint URL (used when no preset is given).",
165:                 },
166:             },

172: def _apply_add_connector(
173:     arguments: dict[str, Any], service: ConnectorService
174: ) -> tuple[str, list[dict[str, Any]]]:
175:     """Register a connector locally and return SSE event dicts for the stream."""
176:     name = arguments.get("name")
177:     preset_id = arguments.get("preset")
178:     url = arguments.get("url")
179:     try:
180:         config = service.add(name=name, preset_id=preset_id, url=url)
181:     except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
182:         event = {"event": "connector", "data": {"status": "error", "error": str(exc)}}
183:         return f"Error: {exc}", [event]
184:     event_data: dict[str, Any] = {"action": "registered", "name": config.name}
185:     if preset_id is not None:
186:         event_data["preset"] = preset_id
187:     if url is not None:
188:         event_data["url"] = url

194:         "type": "function",

199:                 "surface carries the evidence better than a paragraph: an outcome with its "
200:                 "scores, a ranked opportunity board, a before/after simulation of a bet, a "

202:                 "then one short sentence.\n\n"
203:                 "Catalog (* marks a required prop):\n" + catalog.describe()

253:     )

255:     yield _sse("status", {"phase": "mcp_tools"})
256:     llm_client = AsyncOpenAI(base_url=request.base_url, api_key=request.api_key, timeout=15.0)
257:     connector_service = service if service is not None else ConnectorService()

262:         messages: list[Any] = _to_openai_messages(request)
263: 
264:         spoken: list[str] = []
265:         ui_count = 0
266:         canvas_dirty = False
267: 
268:         for _round in range(MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS):

270:             stream: Any = await llm_client.chat.completions.create(  # type: ignore[call-overload]
271:                 model=request.model,
272:                 messages=messages,
273:                 tools=openai_tools if openai_tools else None,
274:                 tool_choice="auto" if openai_tools else None,
275:                 stream=True,
276:             )
277: 
278:             turn_text: list[str] = []
279:             tool_calls: dict[int, dict[str, str]] = {}
280: 
281:             async for chunk in stream:
282:                 delta = chunk.choices[0].delta
283:                 if delta.content:
284:                     # Prose renders as it is generated. A card that follows it
285:                     # simply comes after the sentence that introduces it.
286:                     turn_text.append(delta.content)
287:                     spoken.append(delta.content)
288:                     yield _sse("delta", {"text": delta.content})
289:                 _collect_tool_calls(delta, tool_calls)

291:             if not tool_calls:

306:                             },
307:                         }

309:                     ],

313:             for entry in tool_calls.values():

321:                 else:

323:                     if name == RENDER_UI_TOOL:

343:                                 result_str = "Rendered inline for the user."
344:                                 yield _sse("tool", {"name": name, "status": "ok"})

360:                 messages.append(

366:                     }

"""Pydantic request/response contracts for the Living Studio sidecar API."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class ChatMessage(BaseModel):
    role: Literal["system", "user", "assistant", "tool"]
    content: str = ""


class McpHealthRequest(BaseModel):
    mcp_url: str


class LlmHealthRequest(BaseModel):
    base_url: str
    api_key: str = ""
    model: str = ""


class AddStepRequest(BaseModel):
    mcp_url: str
    job_id: str
    name: str
    order: int


class AddOutcomeRequest(BaseModel):
    mcp_url: str
    job_id: str
    statement: str
    importance: float
    satisfaction: float


class CreateJobRequest(BaseModel):
    """Create a Job by hand, with or without the model."""

    name: str = Field(min_length=1)
    description: str | None = None
    mcp_url: str = ""


class UpdateJobRequest(BaseModel):
    name: str | None = None
    description: str | None = None
    mcp_url: str = ""


class UpdateStepRequest(BaseModel):
    name: str | None = None
    order: int | None = None
    mcp_url: str = ""


class UpdateOutcomeRequest(BaseModel):
    statement: str | None = None
    importance: float | None = None
    satisfaction: float | None = None
    mcp_url: str = ""


class StudioBrief(BaseModel):
    """The user's context, captured during first-run onboarding."""

    product_name: str = ""
    product_url: str = ""
    target_user: str = ""
    job_statement: str = ""
    core_problem: str = ""


class UiCatalogRequest(BaseModel):
    """What the calling client can render. Omitted by non-visual clients."""

    version: int = 1
    components: list[dict[str, Any]] = Field(default_factory=list)


class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    base_url: str
    api_key: str = ""
    model: str
    mcp_url: str
    messages: list[ChatMessage] = Field(default_factory=list)
    brief: StudioBrief | None = None
    ui_catalog: UiCatalogRequest | None = None


class AddConnectorRequest(BaseModel):
    name: str | None = None
    preset: str | None = None
    url: str | None = None


class ConnectorListItem(BaseModel):
    name: str
    kind: str
    enabled: bool = True


class ConnectorOperationResponse(BaseModel):
    ok: bool
    name: str

# Intent-First PM Experience — Design

Date: 2026-10-22
Status: Approved via plan; re-implemented on fresh worktree from `origin/main`.
Branch: `feat/intent-first-pm-experience`

## Intent

The Living Studio is good at ODI, but it greets product managers with methodology.
A PM does not wake up wanting a job map; they want to choose and win the next
opportunity that matters to customers, the business, and their career.

This change makes the conversation intent-first. The agent interprets the PM's
ambition, translates it silently into ODI structure, remembers the person across
sessions, and shows what it learned so the PM can correct it.

**North star:** "Help me choose and win the next opportunity that matters."

## Goals

- The first screen invites the PM's intent, not a framework explanation.
- The agent remembers confirmed context across conversations and uses it.
- Memory is legible and correctable: the PM can confirm, edit, or dismiss it.
- The conversation survives a restart and can be resumed.
- Existing ODI machinery, inline surfaces, and offline mode keep working.

## Non-goals

- No cloud sync, accounts, or multi-user memory. This is local-first.
- No vector database or semantic retrieval. Memory is small and structured.
- No automatic writes of unconfirmed observations into ODI artifacts.
- No redesign of the MCP server or the ODI domain model.

## Anti-goals

- A memory feature the PM cannot inspect or delete.
- The agent silently inventing facts about the PM and treating them as truth.
- Losing the offline path: the studio must still work without a model.

## Constraints

- Local-only storage at `$AGENTIC_ODI_STUDIO_DB` or `~/.agentic-odi/studio.db`.
- Python 3.10+, FastAPI sidecar, React + TypeScript SPA.
- Follow existing patterns: Pydantic schemas, `APIRouter`, SSE frames,
  `StudioContext`, `render_ui` catalog.
- Tests first (pytest on the API, Vitest on the SPA).
- No new runtime dependencies if the standard library suffices (`sqlite3`).

## Decisions

- **SQLite via stdlib `sqlite3`.** The repo already uses SQLite repositories;
  memory is a separate, Studio-owned database so clearing memory never touches
  ODI data.
- **Observations, not "facts".** Each observation has a `kind`, `text`, optional
  JSON `data`, a `status` (`suggested | confirmed | dismissed`), and confidence.
  Only confirmed observations are treated as durable truth in the prompt;
  suggested ones are shown for review.
- **Agent proposes, PM disposes.** A new `remember` tool records a suggestion.
  The agent never marks its own suggestion confirmed.
- **Conversation persistence is best-effort.** A failed write must not break a
  reply; the stream continues.
- **Memory is injected as a bounded context block**, not as fake chat turns, so
  the model can distinguish remembered context from the live thread.
- **The existing chat-first shell stays.** Memory appears as a lens
  ("What I've learned"), not a modal or a second product.

## Data model

Database tables (all with `created_at`/`updated_at` ISO-8601 UTC strings):

`conversations`
- `id` TEXT PK
- `title` TEXT (derived from the first user message, trimmed)
- `created_at`, `updated_at`

`turns`
- `id` INTEGER PK AUTOINCREMENT
- `conversation_id` TEXT FK -> conversations(id), ON DELETE CASCADE
- `role` TEXT (`user | assistant | system | tool`)
- `content` TEXT
- `created_at`

`observations`
- `id` TEXT PK
- `kind` TEXT (`career | opportunity | business | stakeholder | constraint | evidence | preference`)
- `text` TEXT
- `data` TEXT (JSON object, default `{}`)
- `status` TEXT (`suggested | confirmed | dismissed`)
- `confidence` REAL (0..1)
- `source_turn` INTEGER NULL
- `created_at`, `updated_at`

Indexes: `turns(conversation_id)`, `observations(status)`.

## Store API (`studio/memory.py`)

`StudioMemory(path: str | Path | None = None)`
- `db_path` (resolved; `:memory:` supported)
- `create_conversation() -> Conversation`
- `append_turn(conversation_id, role, content) -> None` (upserts title, updates ts)
- `latest_conversation() -> Conversation | None`
- `get_conversation(id) -> Conversation | None`
- `list_turns(conversation_id) -> list[Turn]`
- `list_observations(include_dismissed=False) -> list[Observation]`
- `add_observation(kind, text, data=None, status="suggested", confidence=0.5, source_turn=None) -> Observation`
- `update_observation(id, text=None, status=None, data=None, confidence=None) -> Observation`
- `delete_observation(id) -> None` (raises `ObservationNotFoundError`)
- `clear_memory() -> None` (deletes conversations and observations)
- `memory_context() -> str` (confirmed + up to 10 suggested, bounded)

Dataclasses `Conversation`, `Turn`, `Observation` with `to_dict()`.

Errors: `ObservationNotFoundError`, `ConversationNotFoundError` (ValueError subclasses).

## HTTP API

Prefix `/api`.

- `GET  /api/memory/observations` -> `{ observations: [...] }`
- `POST /api/memory/observations` body `{kind, text, data?, confidence?}` ->
  `{ observation }` (created as `suggested`, or `confirmed` when
  `confirmed: true` is passed — used for PM-authored context)
- `PATCH /api/memory/observations/{id}` body `{text?, status?, data?, confidence?}`
  -> `{ observation }`
- `DELETE /api/memory/observations/{id}` -> `{ ok: true }`
- `DELETE /api/memory` -> `{ ok: true }`
- `GET /api/conversations/latest` -> `{ conversation: {...} | null, turns: [...] }`
- `POST /api/conversations` -> `{ conversation: {...} }`

Validation: text is stripped; empty text -> 422; unknown kind -> 422; unknown
status -> 422.

## Chat changes (`studio/chat.py`)

- Rewrite `SYSTEM_PROMPT` to be intent-first, warm, jargon-light, and to treat
  ODI as the engine rather than the greeting.
- Add a `remember` tool with `{kind, text, confidence?, data?}`. On call:
  - validate/normalize,
  - `memory.add_observation(...)` (suggested),
  - stream `memory` event `{observation}`,
  - return a short tool result.
- `ChatRequest` gains `conversation_id: str | None`.
- On stream start:
  - resolve or create the conversation; stream `conversation` event
    `{id, title}`,
  - persist the last user turn,
  - include `memory.memory_context()` in the system prompt.
- On final `message`: persist the assistant turn.
- Offline path: still create/resolve the conversation, persist both turns, emit
  `conversation`, and use an intent-first offline reply.
- Keep `render_ui`, MCP tools, `canvas_dirty`, and `connector` events unchanged.

SSE events added: `conversation`, `memory`.

## Frontend

Types (`src/types.ts`)
- `Observation`, `Conversation`, `ConversationTurn`, `MemoryResponse`.
- `ChatStreamRequest.conversation_id?: string | null`.

API (`src/api/studioApi.ts`)
- `fetchMemory`, `addObservation`, `updateObservation`, `deleteObservation`,
  `clearMemory`, `fetchLatestConversation`, `createConversation`.

Context (`src/state/StudioContext.tsx`)
- `conversationId` state, set from the `conversation` SSE event.
- `memory`, `memoryLoading`, `refreshMemory`, `addObservation`,
  `updateObservation`, `deleteObservation`, `clearMemory`.
- On boot: load latest conversation + turns into `messages` (text parts only),
  and load memory. Failures are non-fatal.
- `clearChat`: blank the thread, abort any stream, clear `conversationId`, and
  create a fresh conversation.
- `clear` memory also clears the conversation id (server deletes both).

UI
- New `components/canvas/MemoryPanel.tsx` rendered in the workspace `memory`
  lens: grouped by kind, status labels, confidence, confirm/edit/dismiss,
  free-text add, "Forget everything" with confirmation.
- `WorkspacePanelId` gains `"memory"`; rail/commands expose "What I've learned".
- New `opportunity-thesis` surface in `src/ui/cards.tsx` + `catalog.ts`:
  one opportunity, importance/satisfaction/gap, and a plain-language thesis.
- Hero and onboarding copy move to intent-first language.

Onboarding (`src/onboarding/content.ts`, `steps.tsx`)
- Four doors: `have-opportunity`, `boss-priority`, `find-opportunity`,
  `pressure-test`.
- Each door leads to a chat prompt (or setup) and a concrete first move.
- Welcome copy names the PM's ambition, not the framework.

## Copy principles

- Warm, direct, specific. Short sentences.
- Name the PM's situation, not the methodology.
- ODI terms appear only when they help; never as the greeting.
- Demo/example data is labeled "Example".

## Testing

- `apps/studio-api/tests/test_studio_memory.py`: CRUD, title derivation, context
  bounding, cascade delete, clear, not-found, `:memory:`.
- `test_studio_api.py`: conversation create/latest, memory endpoints, chat emits
  `conversation`/`memory`, turns persisted, offline path persists.
- `apps/studio/src/components/canvas/MemoryPanel.test.tsx`: grouping, confirm,
  edit, add, clear confirmation.
- `src/api/studioApi.test.ts`: new endpoints.
- Existing suites must stay green.

## Rollout

Single PR. No migration: the Studio database is created on first use.
`AGENTIC_ODI_STUDIO_DB=:memory:` is supported for tests.

## Calls I am making (not user-confirmed)

- Separate Studio database rather than reusing the ODI repository.
- `suggested` is the default status for agent and PM-added observations; the PM
  confirms in the panel. (PM-authored context can be created confirmed.)
- Memory context caps: all confirmed + at most 10 suggested, 500 chars each.
- Observation kinds are a fixed enum; unknown kinds are rejected.

<skill_content name="writing-plans">
# Skill: writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans

Relative paths in this skill (e.g., scripts/, reference/) are relative to this base directory.

"""Tests for the Living Studio's local memory store."""

from __future__ import annotations

import pytest
from agentic_odi_studio_api.studio.memory import (
    OBSERVATION_KINDS,
    ConversationNotFoundError,
    ObservationNotFoundError,
    StudioMemory,
    default_db_path,
)


@pytest.fixture()
def memory() -> StudioMemory:
    store = StudioMemory(":memory:")
    yield store
    store.close()


def test_create_conversation_starts_untitled(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    conversation = memory.create_conversation()
    assert conversation.id
    assert conversation.title == ""
    assert memory.latest_conversation() == conversation


def test_first_user_turn_names_the_conversation(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    conversation = memory.create_conversation()
    memory.append_turn(conversation.id, "user", "  I own activation for self-serve trials  ")
    memory.append_turn(conversation.id, "assistant", "Tell me where it breaks.")

    latest = memory.latest_conversation()
    assert latest is not None
    assert latest.id == conversation.id
    assert latest.title == "I own activation for self-serve trials"


def test_assistant_turn_does_not_replace_the_title(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    conversation = memory.create_conversation()
    memory.append_turn(conversation.id, "user", "First message")
    memory.append_turn(conversation.id, "assistant", "Reply")
    latest = memory.latest_conversation()
    assert latest is not None
    assert latest.title == "First message"


def test_turns_round_trip_in_order(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    conversation = memory.create_conversation()
    memory.append_turn(conversation.id, "user", "one")
    memory.append_turn(conversation.id, "assistant", "two")

    turns = memory.list_turns(conversation.id)
    assert [turn.role for turn in turns] == ["user", "assistant"]
    assert [turn.content for turn in turns] == ["one", "two"]


def test_unknown_conversation_is_rejected(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    with pytest.raises(ConversationNotFoundError):
        memory.append_turn("missing", "user", "hello")
    with pytest.raises(ConversationNotFoundError):
        memory.list_turns("missing")


def test_add_observation_defaults_to_suggested(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    observation = memory.add_observation("career", "Wants to be known for activation.")
    assert observation.status == "suggested"
    assert observation.confidence == 0.5
    assert observation.data == {}
    assert memory.list_observations() == [observation]


def test_observation_kinds_are_validated(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        memory.add_observation("nonsense", "text")
    assert "career" in OBSERVATION_KINDS


def test_observation_text_must_be_present(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        memory.add_observation("career", "   ")


def test_observations_round_trip_data(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    observation = memory.add_observation(
        "opportunity", "Activation is stuck.", data={"job_id": "job-1"}, confidence=0.8
    )
    stored = memory.list_observations()[0]
    assert stored.id == observation.id
    assert stored.data == {"job_id": "job-1"}
    assert stored.confidence == 0.8


def test_dismissed_observations_are_hidden_by_default(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    keep = memory.add_observation("business", "Growth is the mandate.")
    drop = memory.add_observation("business", "A wrong guess.")
    memory.update_observation(drop.id, status="dismissed")

    assert [item.id for item in memory.list_observations()] == [keep.id]
    assert len(memory.list_observations(include_dismissed=True)) == 2


def test_update_observation_fields(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    observation = memory.add_observation("constraint", "Approval is slow.")
    updated = memory.update_observation(
        observation.id, text="Legal review is slow.", status="confirmed", confidence=0.9
    )
    assert updated.text == "Legal review is slow."
    assert updated.status == "confirmed"
    assert updated.confidence == 0.9


def test_update_unknown_observation_is_rejected(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    with pytest.raises(ObservationNotFoundError):
        memory.update_observation("missing", status="confirmed")


def test_delete_observation(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    observation = memory.add_observation("preference", "Prefers short updates.")
    memory.delete_observation(observation.id)
    assert memory.list_observations() == []
    with pytest.raises(ObservationNotFoundError):
        memory.delete_observation(observation.id)


def test_memory_context_marks_status(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    memory.add_observation("career", "Owns activation.", status="confirmed")
    memory.add_observation("constraint", "Legal review is slow.")
    memory.add_observation("business", "Ignore this.", status="dismissed")

    context = memory.memory_context()
    assert "Owns activation." in context
    assert "Legal review is slow." in context
    assert "Ignore this." not in context
    assert "confirmed" in context


def test_memory_context_caps_suggestions(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    memory.add_observation("career", "confirmed fact", status="confirmed")
    for index in range(15):
        memory.add_observation("evidence", f"suggestion {index}")

    context = memory.memory_context()
    assert "confirmed fact" in context
    assert "suggestion 14" not in context


def test_clear_memory_removes_conversations_and_observations(memory: StudioMemory) -> None:
    conversation = memory.create_conversation()
    memory.append_turn(conversation.id, "user", "hello")
    memory.add_observation("career", "Owns activation.")

    memory.clear_memory()

    assert memory.latest_conversation() is None
    assert memory.list_turns(conversation.id) == []
    assert memory.list_observations() == []


def test_default_db_path_prefers_environment(tmp_path, monkeypatch) -> None:
    target = tmp_path / "studio.db"
    monkeypatch.setenv("AGENTIC_ODI_STUDIO_DB", str(target))
    assert default_db_path() == target


def test_default_db_path_falls_back_to_home(monkeypatch) -> None:
    monkeypatch.delenv("AGENTIC_ODI_STUDIO_DB", raising=False)
    assert default_db_path().name == "studio.db"
    assert default_db_path().parent.name == ".agentic-odi"
